short: Shakespeare’s tragedy of the prince of Denmark.
note: Hamlet I.1 includes Marcellus’s account of Christmas nights, when the cock sings and harmful spirits and astral influences lose their power. The passage preserves beliefs about the protective sanctity of Christmas.

short: Fermented green fodder stored for livestock.
note: Grass or other green crops preserved by fermentation with air largely excluded, then fed to farm animals.

short: A red-and-white cattle breed from England.
note: Hereford cattle originated in Herefordshire, England. They are a beef breed characteristically red-bodied with white faces and other white markings.

short: A cattle breed developed on Texas’s King Ranch.
note: Santa Gertrudis cattle were developed at the King Ranch from Shorthorn and Brahman ancestry. The established breed is approximately five-eighths Shorthorn and three-eighths Brahman.

sources.label: Oklahoma State University · Santa Gertrudis cattle

short: Irish fairy folk, associated with ancient mounds.
note: Sidhe is an older spelling connected with Irish sí, a fairy mound. Aos sí denotes the supernatural people believed to inhabit such mounds.
A colloquial name for remote, thinly settled country. The English word derives from Tagalog bundok, meaning mountain.

short: Possibly an Arabic expression for the land of Egypt.
note: Possibly Arabic bilād Maṣr, the country of Egypt; barr Maṣr likewise means the land of Egypt. Older English phrasebooks transcribe the latter as berr masr.

sources.label: Captain C. A. Thimm · Egyptian Self-Taught

short: Texas cattle noted for their long horns.
note: Texas Longhorn cattle descend from cattle brought to North America by Spanish settlers. The hardy breed became important to the ranching economy of the American Southwest.

sources.label: Oklahoma State University: Texas Longhorn cattle

short: Possibly the cross-shaped marking of a donkey.
note: Possibly the cross-shaped marking on a donkey’s back. Christian folk tradition explains the mark by the donkey’s carrying Jesus into Jerusalem.

sources.label: F. Edward Hulme: Natural History, Lore and Legend, pp. 184–186

short: Possibly the Christmas legend of speaking animals.
note: Possibly an echo of the folk belief that animals gain human speech at midnight on Christmas Eve and speak about Christ’s birth.

short: Possibly the shepherds visiting the newborn Jesus.
note: Possibly an echo of Luke 2:8–20: shepherds keeping night watch hear an angel announce Christ’s birth, then visit Mary, Joseph, and the child lying in a manger.

short: Possibly the Magi who bring gifts to the Christ child.
note: Possibly an echo of the learned visitors in Matthew 2:1–12. The Magi follow a star and offer gold, frankincense, and myrrh; Matthew names three gifts but does not state how many Magi there were.

sources.label: Matthew 2:1–12, United States Conference of Catholic Bishops
